text: Temporal distinguishes workflow retries from activity retries. Workflow code is deterministic and replayed from history on worker crashes — it is never retried at the workflow level by Temporal itself. Activities, in contrast, are at-least-once units of work; their RetryPolicy is what users typically mean by 'retry'. The RetryPolicy fields are initial_interval, backoff_coefficient, maximum_interval, maximum_attempts, and non_retryable_error_types.

Temporal workflow functions must be deterministic. The same workflow code with the same history must produce the same sequence of commands every time it is replayed. Forbidden operations inside workflow code: time.Now, random sources, direct I/O, native goroutines/threads, map iteration order. Use workflow.Now, workflow.NewRandom, workflow.ExecuteActivity for all of these.

Signals are how external code injects information into a running workflow. The workflow exposes a signal channel via workflow.GetSignalChannel(ctx, name). The sender uses client.SignalWorkflow(ctx, workflowID, runID, signalName, payload). Signals are durable and survive worker crashes; they're the right primitive for human-approval gates.

Temporal task queues are first-class routing primitives. Workers register against a named task queue; the server dispatches workflow and activity tasks to whichever worker has registered the type. A polyglot setup like HarnessFlow's runs a Go worker and a Python worker on the same task queue — the Go worker registers the workflow function, the Python worker registers the activities, and Temporal routes by task type.

Child workflows let you decompose long-running workflows into reusable units. Parent invokes via workflow.ExecuteChildWorkflow; the child has its own workflow ID, history, and retry behavior. Use them when a sub-procedure has its own lifecycle (own retries, own cancellation scope) — not as a substitute for activities.

Claude's tool use feature lets the model decide when to call external tools by emitting structured JSON. Tools are described to the model via the tools parameter on messages.create; the model returns tool_use content blocks that the application executes and feeds back as tool_result. This pattern enables agentic workflows without surrendering control over execution to a third-party orchestrator.

Anthropic introduced computer use in October 2024 — a Claude variant that can read a screen, decide on actions, and emit pointer/keyboard commands. Computer use is delivered as a tool in the standard tool-use API; integrators provide a screenshot and receive back a structured action. The capability is positioned as 'agent infrastructure' rather than a finished product.

Constitutional AI (CAI) is Anthropic's approach to alignment: the model is trained to critique and revise its own outputs against a written 'constitution' of principles. The technique was introduced in 2022 and underpins Claude's refusal and helpfulness behavior. CAI moves human judgment up the abstraction ladder — from labeling individual responses to debating principles.

Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) commits to specific AI Safety Levels (ASL) with safety capabilities required at each level. ASL-2 covers current models; ASL-3 introduces stricter security and deployment commitments and is triggered by specific capability thresholds, not by calendar dates. The RSP is a public, voluntary commitment.

Anthropic's engineering team has repeatedly observed that AI agents need infrastructure — durable state, retries, observability, and human-approval surfaces — in the same way distributed systems do. Off-the-shelf LLM orchestration libraries often hide this layer behind abstractions that leak in production. Building agent platforms on workflow engines like Temporal is the increasingly recommended pattern.

OpenTelemetry semantic conventions standardize attribute names across telemetry signals. They reduce vendor lock-in: instrumenting with semconv keys means any compliant backend (Jaeger, Tempo, Datadog, Honeycomb) can analyze your traces without custom mapping. New conventions like the GenAI namespace (gen_ai.system, gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens) are added as use cases stabilize.

The GenAI semantic conventions, stabilized through 2024-2025, define attributes for LLM calls. Required: gen_ai.system (e.g. 'openai', 'anthropic'), gen_ai.request.model. Recommended: gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens, gen_ai.response.finish_reasons, gen_ai.operation.name. The spec deliberately omits cost, leaving that to vendor-specific attributes.

OpenTelemetry uses W3C Trace Context for cross-process trace propagation. The traceparent HTTP header carries trace_id, span_id, sampled, and version. SDKs install a global TextMapPropagator that extracts traceparent on incoming requests and injects it on outgoing calls; this is how a single trace ID spans services written in different languages.

OpenTelemetry baggage propagates user-defined key-value pairs alongside the trace context. Baggage is intended for cross-cutting metadata (tenant ID, user ID, experiment variant) — not for arbitrary data, which would inflate every downstream request. Backends typically expose baggage as span attributes if the application copies it explicitly.

The BatchSpanProcessor buffers exported spans and flushes them in batches to reduce export overhead. Default schedule_delay_millis is 5 seconds. On shutdown, force_flush MUST be called before TracerProvider.shutdown — without it, the last few spans may never reach the collector, which is a common cause of 'I see all spans except the final ones'.

OpenTelemetry sampling decides which traces are recorded. Head-based sampling decides at trace start (e.g. ParentBased(TraceIdRatioBased(0.1))); tail-based sampling decides after the trace completes (e.g. keep all errors, sample 1% of successes). Tail sampling requires a collector-side decision component, which is heavier ops but better for low-volume high-value traces.

HarnessFlow is a polyglot workflow orchestration platform for AI agents. A Go orchestrator (apps/api) accepts workflow YAML, validates it against a JSON Schema, and compiles it into deterministic Temporal Workflow functions. Python workers (apps/worker) register against the same Temporal cluster and execute activities — llm_call, retrieve, tool_call, verify — that call OpenAI/Anthropic via an in-house LLMClient (no LangChain).

HarnessFlow is OpenTelemetry-native. Trace context propagates Go -> Temporal -> Python -> LLM-call as a single trace ID in Jaeger. The LLMClient emits OTel GenAI semantic-convention spans (gen_ai.system, gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens). Cost is recorded as the custom harnessflow.cost_usd_cents attribute pending an OTel-standard cost field.

HarnessFlow's CI/CD model is eval-gated PRs. A GitHub Action triggers on PRs that modify packages/examples/workflows/*.yaml; it spins up docker-compose, runs the eval suite against the modified workflow vs main, posts a markdown comparison comment, and blocks merge if scores regress. The same gate is reused by the autonomous workflow-mutation agent (Week 14).

HarnessFlow does not use LangChain. The in-house LLMClient is ~200 lines that handle provider routing, declared model fallback, OTel GenAI semconv spans, and per-call cost accounting. LangChain's frequent breaking changes and hidden retry behavior complicate OTel instrumentation. The decision is documented as ADR-0003 (skip-langchain) in Project-Documentation/decisions/.
